title: I bundled a fully local LLM inside my Unity game. No internet, no cloud, no API key. The conversation is the gameplay.
author: MorphLand
selftext:
My game 'Simulation Simulator' is a campfire conversation game about DMT, simulation theory, and a friend with a computer monitor for a head. The game is bundled with a local LLM and every conversation is unique. 5 endings you can reach totally based on how you interact naturally with the AI. One is a romance ending! Everything in the clip is totally organic and unscripted.

  
Trying to use AI for good. Not trying to toot my own horn but I honestly haven't seen the use of LLM tech inside games to this extent yet. I'm sure people much smarter than me must be trying though. For NPCs & world building, this seems like a logical next step.

  
I even wanted to do text to speech audio and automatic translation. The only thing really preventing it right now is processing time on local machines. Those extra layers would add like 10-20 seconds of calls per exchange so it just breaks the game. If processing gets faster/better, I can imagine whole towns of NPCs with memories, that have no scripted dialogue at all and change over time. 

  
In my game here, you argue with an LLM and can attempt to prove that reality itself is a simulation. It's really a philosophical experiment more than a game. It can get trippy trying to prove you do or don't exist. 

  
Anyway, demo for Simulation Simulator is out on steam if you want to try for yourself. Let's talk using AI for good in games!

comments.author: kal101246
comments.body: How do you balance the use of deterministic behavior vs llm use? I'm asking because what if the person playing the game is on an older slower device and doesn't have much resources available for your local llm to use?

replies.author: MorphLand
replies.body: Well first of all it's really not he most intensive system. I settled on an older LLM after a LOT of testing. this was developed on a macbook air and the response time you see in the clip is real gameplay. On worse machines, yeah, you'll get frame rate drops while it's thinking and response times will be longer. But I'm up front about that. This is really an experiment more than anything.

replies.author: kal101246
replies.body: Yeah that could be a cool part of the game design, introducing "lag" or delay malfunction to make it feel realistic lol

comments.author: Afraid-Act424
comments.body:
Which SLM do you use?

You can do local TTS/STT with low latency using optimized models (Kitten TTS, Kokoro, Piper...) and for STT, low-latency models from Banafo [https://huggingface.co/Banafo/Kroko-ASR](https://huggingface.co/Banafo/Kroko-ASR)

comments.author: Revelation12Studios
comments.body: Interesting. Are there super lightweight models that can be used to simulate a ton of players talking in an mmorpg?

replies.author: MorphLand
replies.body: Not yet, but i can definitely see this being possible in the future. Even two lightweight LLMs running at once during a game would be enough to explode most consumer computers

replies.author: Revelation12Studios
replies.body: Would one LLM operating as multiple player bots, saying game-appropriate things, without real players interacting with them in chat, be feasible?

replies.author: MorphLand
replies.body: It’s feasible but prone to error. You’d basically use code to swap out personality and memory documents but I definitely haven’t seen it done yet. I’m working on a small town next with three people in it as a test.
